ak-fix.tagline: Fix bugs, errors, test failures, and broken CI. Prove the cause first.
ak-fix.summary: ak:fix takes a concrete symptom (error message, failing test, red CI, log error, UI bug) to a verified fix. It requires a proven root cause before editing, picks a quick/standard/deep route by complexity, then reruns the original failing command plus affected caller checks. Output: the fix, a regression test when useful, a cause/changes/verification report, and an automatic journal entry.
howItWorks: Captures or reuses outcome, constraints, non-goals, and acceptance criteria; records the pre-fix failing command.
Picks a mode: --auto by default; without a flag on a non-obvious issue, asks Autonomous / Human-in-the-loop / Quick fix.
Scouts with ak:scout or 2-3 parallel Explore subagents to map affected files, tests, and recent git changes.
Diagnoses with ak:debug; switches to ak:problem-solving after 2+ failed hypotheses.
Passes a root-cause hard gate: verbatim symptom, repro, expected vs actual, file:line cause, why now, blast radius.
Routes by complexity: Simple (1 file, type/lint) → quick; Moderate (2-5 files) → standard 6 phases; Complex (5+ files, architecture) → deep 9 phases.
Deep route runs scout/diagnose/research in parallel, then ak:brainstorm picks a direction and planner writes a plan.
With --ultra, generates 5 read-only candidate fix-plans after diagnosis; a verifier picks one or rejects all.
Implements a minimal fix at the root cause, following existing patterns.
Reruns the pre-fix command, adds a regression test, sweeps side effects, runs typecheck/lint/build/test.
On failure, returns to diagnosis; after 3 failed attempts, stops to review architecture with the user.
Reviews by risk: code-reviewer subagent when allowed, otherwise a self-review of the diff.
Finalizes: syncs the plan, updates affected docs, reports results, runs /ak:journal unless opted out; commits only with permission.
useWhen: A concrete error needs fixing: type error, lint error, failing test, logged exception.
CI or GitHub Actions is red and the pipeline must go green.
A UI or visual bug needs a fix verified in a browser.
Several independent bugs with separate file ownership can be fixed in parallel with --parallel.
A hard bug has competing fixes and you want the best plan via --ultra.
avoidWhen: You only want to investigate the cause without fixing: use ak:debug.
The work is a new feature or known non-bug scope: use ak:cook.
You want to improve a measurable metric over many iterations: use ak:loop.
You only need to run tests or check coverage: use ak:test.
You want the full issue-to-PR pipeline: use ak:vibe.

params.name: [issue]
params.desc: Error description, message, failing test, or CI link. If missing, the skill narrows it down from context.

params.name: --auto
params.desc: Default. Proceeds through fix and verify within allowed scope; asks only for key decisions, contract reversals, or unapproved destructive actions.

params.name: --review
params.desc: Human-in-the-loop: pauses for approval at each major step. Recommended for production, security, or system-wide bugs.

params.name: --quick
params.desc: Lean cause-aligned fix: scout → diagnose → fix → verify+prevent → review. Escalates to standard/deep if architecture decisions appear. Conflicts with --ultra.

params.name: --parallel
params.desc: Fixes several independent issues with separate file ownership via parallel delegation, when the runtime supports it. Conflicts with --ultra.

params.name: --ultra
params.desc: After diagnosis, generates exactly 5 read-only candidate fix-plans; a verifier picks the winner by cause alignment, blast radius, minimality, verifiability. Reject-all stops. Hard-stops with --quick or --parallel.

params.name: --advice
params.desc: Runs under kongming supervision: after each step, when stuck, on verify failure, and before high-risk decisions. Kongming advises only; it writes no code.

params.name: --skip-journal
params.desc: Skips the automatic /ak:journal step. Precedence: flag > project config > user config > default true. Also skipped when journal.auto=false.

The skill never commits or pushes; use ak:git or ak:ship afterward.

Report of cause, changed paths, verification, limitations

ak-debug.tagline: Investigate systematically and prove the root cause before any fix.
ak-debug.summary: ak:debug investigates failures at code level (failing tests, bugs, builds) and system level (server errors, CI/CD, performance, databases, logs). Core rule: no fix without a root-cause investigation, and no "done" without fresh verification evidence. Output: a diagnosis with file:line evidence, ruled-out hypotheses, blast radius, and a verification plan.
howItWorks: Classifies the problem and loads the matching reference: code bug, deep stack error, system incident, CI/CD, performance, or frontend.
Code bugs follow 4 phases in order: Root Cause Investigation → Pattern Analysis → Hypothesis Testing → Implementation.
Root-cause tracing walks the call stack back to the original trigger; scripts/find-polluter.sh bisects test pollution.
System incidents follow 5 steps: assess, collect data, analyze, identify root cause, develop solution.
Collects logs via gh CLI, psql, and structured log queries.
With --ultra, builds one immutable evidence packet and runs 5 read-only diagnoses in parallel; a verifier picks one or rejects all.
After the root cause is known, adds defensive checks only at boundaries that distinguish the cause or protect the fixed contract.
Frontend files trigger browser checks (ak:agent-browser, ak:chrome-profile, Chrome MCP): screenshots and console errors.
Tracks 3+ step or parallel investigations in a task surface or the active plan.
Verification iron law: run the command, read the output, then claim the result.
useWhen: A test fails or behavior is wrong and the cause is unknown.
A CI/CD pipeline fails and GitHub Actions logs need reading.
The system is slow: slow queries, high latency, resource exhaustion.
A server or production incident spans components and needs a diagnostic report.
Test pollution (a test fails only with the full suite) needs bisecting.
avoidWhen: The cause is known and you just need a fix: use ak:fix (it calls debug when needed).
You have a diagnosis and need to compare solutions: use ak:brainstorm.
You only need to find related files: use ak:scout.
You are stuck on framing, not missing evidence: use ak:problem-solving.

params.name: [error or issue description]
params.desc: Error description, message, stack trace, or symptom to investigate.

params.name: --ultra
params.desc: Best-of-5 diagnosis: one immutable evidence packet, 5 independent read-only diagnoses, a verifier picks one intact or rejects all. The winning cause still needs fresh verification before a fix. Reject-all hard-stops with reasons.

examples.note: Suspected test pollution: use root-cause tracing and find-polluter.sh.

examples.note: Investigate CI logs via gh CLI.

examples.note: Hard bug, many hypotheses: 5 independent diagnoses plus a verifier.

tips: Watch for red flags: "quick fix now, investigate later", "try changing X", "probably X", "seems fixed".
A minimal repro and real logs cut investigation rounds and tokens.
--ultra fans out analysis only; any fix still runs once after the cause is verified.
Frontend screenshots and console checks need a browser tool (agent-browser or Chrome MCP).
Debug does not batch-fix; switch to /ak:fix once the root cause is proven.
artifacts: Diagnostic report (when needed) per reporting standards
Updated active plan for multi-step investigations

ak-test.tagline: Run, create, optimize, and audit test suites with structured QA reports.
ak-test.summary: ak:test covers code-level tests (Jest/Vitest/Mocha, pytest, go test, cargo test, flutter test), browser UI tests, coverage, build checks, and QA reports. Subcommands ui, create, optimize, and audit test websites, build suites, cut CI cost, or expose deceptive tests. All work follows 11 practical testing principles; failing tests are never skipped, mocked, or cheated.
howItWorks: With no argument, asks which operation to run: default, ui, create, optimize, or audit. With context, starts immediately.
Loads the practical testing principles first; they govern scope, layer, environment, and execution for every change and report.
Default: scopes from recent changes → runs the narrowest check → runs the suite → analyzes failures → coverage → UI tests → report.
ui [url]: tests a site via ak:agent-browser, ak:chrome-profile (real logged-in Chrome), or the project's Playwright/Vitest/k6.
UI checks cover screenshots, responsiveness, accessibility, forms, and console errors.
create: scouts code and docs, builds a coverage matrix, designs first, then writes and verifies the suite.
optimize: parallel scouts analyze CI, git history, code, and docs, then speed up tests at equal safety behind mandatory gates.
audit: parallel scouts find tests written only to pass, skipped or commented tests, duplicates, stale and insecure tests; reports only.
--interview lists each proposed change with a one-line reason and applies only approved groups.
--advice consults kongming after analysis, before applying suite/CI changes, and when stuck.
--ultra runs 5 read-only candidates plus a verifier; create/optimize pick one design, audit merges verified findings.
Hands screenshots to ak:ai-multimodal, bugs to ak:debug, and hard failures to ak:fable-thinking.
useWhen: You just implemented or fixed something and need to confirm nothing broke before committing.
You want to test a website UI: responsive, accessibility, console errors, forms, logged-in routes.
The project lacks a test suite covering main flows (create).
CI is too slow or costly and you want less time without losing coverage (optimize).
You suspect the suite is unreliable: skipped, fake, or stale tests (audit).
You need a final quality gate before commit/push: build and coverage thresholds.
avoidWhen: A test fails and you need to find and fix the cause: use ak:fix or ak:debug.
You need edge cases or QA scenarios before coding: use ak:scenario.
You need deep load, visual regression, or cross-browser testing: use or combine with ak:web-testing.
You want a code quality review, not test runs: use ak:code-review.

params.name: audit [scope]
params.desc: Checks suite and CI; reports ranked, evidence-backed findings with fix suggestions. Fixes only when separately requested.

params.name: --advice
params.desc: With create/optimize/audit: kongming advises after analysis, before suite/CI changes, and when stuck. Never overrides failing-test rules or CI safety gates.

params.desc: With create/optimize/audit: best-of-5 analysis/design (5 read-only candidates + 1 verifier). Create/optimize take one winning design; audit takes the union of verified findings. Combines with --advice and --interview.

params.desc: With create/optimize/audit: lists each proposed change with a one-line reason, asks one decision per group, applies only approved changes.

Coverage gained by loosening assertions is a regression; tests run sequentially unless there is a reason.

ak-code-review.tagline: Evidence-based code review for pending changes, PRs, commits, or a whole codebase.
ak-code-review.summary: ak:code-review checks the requested scope against spec, regression paths, security, and repo conventions. Findings come with file/line, impact, and evidence. It detects the input type itself: PR number, commit hash, --pending, codebase, or codebase parallel. Review-only mode never edits, posts comments, or merges.
howItWorks: Resolves input left to right: PR #/URL → gh pr view + diff; 7-40 hex hash → git show; --pending → git diff HEAD.
No argument with recent changes uses the default target; with nothing to review, asks for a target.
Prefers PR over commit when ambiguous and notes the assumption; reports clearly if the target does not exist.
Sends changed files to an edge-case scout, then runs Stage 1 spec compliance (if a plan/spec exists) and Stage 2 code quality.
Operations: review-only, receiving feedback (verify findings before accepting), or fixing when allowed, then re-reviewing.
codebase: parallel researchers, /ak:scout, parallel code-reviewers, and a planner writing an improvement plan; asks before commit/push.
codebase parallel: lists edge cases, groups them into at most 6 buckets, one code-reviewer per bucket.
--ultra runs Stage 1 once and fans Stage 2 to 5 read-only reviewers; a verifier returns the deduplicated union.
--advice consults kongming after each stage, when stuck, and before high-risk verdicts.
Uses a checklist for risky changes and reuses checks when revision, input, and environment are unchanged.
useWhen: You want to review staged/unstaged changes before committing (--pending).
You need to review a GitHub PR by number or URL.
You want to check whether a specific commit caused a regression.
You need a whole-codebase audit for bugs, security risks, and tech debt.
You received review feedback and need to verify findings before fixing.
avoidWhen: You want to post comments to GitHub, fix, and merge: use ak:review-pr.
You only need security, secret, or dependency scanning: use ak:security.
You need a UI guideline compliance review: use ak:ui-ux-pro-max.
You want to ship a finished branch to a PR: use ak:ship (it runs a 2-pass review).

params.name: COMMIT
params.desc: 7-40 character hex commit hash; reviews the commit diff via git show. The commit must exist locally.

params.name: --pending
params.desc: Reviews staged + unstaged changes vs HEAD (git diff HEAD); asks for a short intent since there is no commit message.

params.name: codebase
params.desc: Full-codebase scan: parallel researchers and code-reviewers, a planner builds an improvement plan, then a report and commit/push offer.

params.name: codebase parallel
params.desc: Multi-reviewer audit: lists edge cases first, splits into at most 6 groups, one code-reviewer per group. Conflicts with --ultra.

params.name: --ultra
params.desc: Best-of-5 Stage 2: 5 independent read-only reviewers, verifier returns the deduplicated union of verified findings. Works with #PR/COMMIT/--pending/codebase and --yagni; hard-stops with codebase parallel.

params.name: --advice
params.desc: Kongming advises after Stage 1, after Stage 2, when stuck, and before high-risk verdicts. Does not override evidence rules or the ultra/parallel conflict.

params.name: --yagni
params.desc: Reviewers keep your full requested scope by default; --yagni adds recommendations to cut scope not needed for the outcome.

ak-ship.tagline: One command: test, review, version, changelog, commit, push, and open a PR.
ak-ship.summary: ak:ship runs a 14-step pipeline that takes a feature branch to a PR, with optional review-merge and a build-in-public post. It detects official mode (into main/master) or beta mode (into dev/beta/develop), plus the test runner, version file, and changelog format. Output: the PR URL and a per-step status table.
howItWorks: Normalizes the mode token: official|stable|main → official, beta|dev|next → beta; unknown tokens stop and ask.
Without a token, infers mode from the branch name (feature/hotfix/bugfix → official; dev/beta/experiment → beta), else asks.
Step 1 pre-flight: checks branch and status, aborts if already on the target, analyzes the diff.
Step 2 links or creates the related GitHub issue; Step 3 merges origin/<target> and stops on unresolvable conflicts.
Step 4 runs tests via the tester subagent; Step 5 runs a 2-pass review (critical + informational) via code-reviewer.
Step 6 bumps version (patch auto, major/minor asks); Step 7 generates the changelog; both skip silently if files are missing.
Step 8 journal and Step 9 docs update run in the background (docs only in official); Step 9b marks the plan completed.
Steps 10-12: conventional commit, git push -u (never force-push), gh pr create with a 7-section evidence body, link PR to plan.
Step 13 (--merge) runs ak:review-pr <PR> --fix --reply --merge to review, fix, reply, merge, and wait for green CI.
Step 14 (--social) drafts and saves a build-in-public journal, then posts to configured channels; dry-run without --yes-post.
--both runs the beta stage first, then a gated stable stage.
useWhen: A feature branch is done and you want one command to test, review, commit, push, and open a PR.
You ship to dev/beta with a lighter pipeline that skips docs.
You want the PR auto-reviewed, fixed, merged, and CI-verified (--merge).
You need beta first, then a controlled promotion to stable (--both).
You want a build-in-public post after the PR is green (--social).
avoidWhen: You only need a plain commit/push: use ak:git.
Code is unfinished or tests are red from an unfixed bug: use ak:fix first.
You only need to review/merge an existing PR: use ak:review-pr.
You want to deploy an app to hosting: use ak:deploy.
You want the full issue → plan → code → PR flow: use ak:vibe.

params.name: official | stable | main
params.desc: Normalized to official: ships to the detected default branch (main/master) with the full pipeline, including docs and journal.

params.name: beta | dev | next
params.desc: Normalized to beta: ships to the detected dev branch (dev/beta/develop) with a lighter pipeline that skips docs. Without a token: base main/master → official, else beta.

params.name: --both
params.desc: Ships beta, then a gated stable stage. Overrides the mode token with one warning. Combines with --advice, --merge, skip flags; --dry-run simulates only beta. Stable never force-pushes or bypasses branch protection.

params.name: --advice
params.desc: Kongming supervises: after pre-flight, after test + review (before version/commit/push/PR), when stuck, and before high-risk decisions. Passed on to ak:review-pr with --merge.

params.name: --merge
params.desc: After the PR, runs ak:review-pr <PR> --fix --reply --merge (plus --advice if set). Claims merged/green only when Verdict=Approve, Merge=merged, CI=green.

params.name: --skip-tests
params.desc: Skips Step 4 tests; use only with passing-test evidence on the same revision.

params.name: --skip-review
params.desc: Skips the pre-landing review (Step 5); the ak:review-pr review under --merge still runs.

params.name: --skip-journal
params.desc: Skips Step 8 journal; also honors journal.auto=false. Note: it also skips the whole --social step.

params.name: --skip-docs
params.desc: Skips Step 9 docs update.

params.name: --social
params.desc: Opt-in: after the PR (and Step 13), drafts a build-in-public journal (Why this / What changed / The tricky bit / What's next), saves it via ak journal create, and posts it. Refuses on red CI; quotes only COLLABORATOR/MEMBER/OWNER comments.

params.desc: Required with --social to actually post; without it, the social step only renders per-channel drafts (dry-run).

params.name: --yes-post-private
params.desc: Required with --social --yes-post on private repos: a second confirmation to post about non-public work.

params.name: --dry-run

Unrelated dirty files stay untouched; only this task's files are committed.
Journal and docs run in the background; skip them with --skip-journal/--skip-docs to save tokens.
--social is dry-run by default; real posting needs --yes-post (and --yes-post-private for private repos).
artifacts: GitHub pull request with a 7-section evidence body
Version bump and CHANGELOG (if the repo has them)
Plan marked completed with linked PR

ak-loop.tagline: Automated optimization loop: try changes, measure a metric, keep or revert via git.
ak-loop.summary: ak:loop improves a measurable metric (coverage, bundle size, ESLint errors, Lighthouse) by repeating Modify → Verify → Keep/Discard. Each iteration commits one atomic change before measuring. Input is a config block (Goal, Scope, Verify, optional fields); output is git history of kept changes, loop-results.tsv, and a final report. Manual invocation only; needs a git repo with a clean working tree.
howItWorks: Parses the config from the message; asks once for any missing required fields (Goal, Scope, Verify).
Screens the Verify command: rejects rm -rf /, fork bombs, curl | sh; warns on unknown hosts, embedded credentials, sudo/chmod 777.
Phase 0: checks prerequisites and a clean tree, records the baseline. Guard must pass at baseline; fix it rather than loosen it.
Phase 1 reviews git history and past results; Phase 2 picks one atomic change describable in one sentence without "and".
Phase 3 edits only within Scope (Guard files stay read-only); Phase 4 commits BEFORE verifying, so git is the memory.
Phase 5 runs Verify within Timeout (default 30s); crashes and timeouts are discarded safely.
Phase 5.5 runs Guard if set: on failure, revert, retry twice, then discard as guard-failed.
Phase 6 decides via a matrix using Noise, Min-Delta, and Direction; Discard uses git revert (git reset --hard only as fallback).
Phase 7 appends a TSV row to loop-results.tsv (iter, timestamp, metric, delta, kept, description).
Phase 8: 5 consecutive discards → change strategy; 10 → stop and report; after Iterations, write a final report.
useWhen: You want test coverage in a folder raised to a specific threshold.
You want bundle size below a target number.
You want ESLint or type errors driven to zero over many small steps.
You have a shell-measurable performance metric and want automated experiments with rollback.
avoidWhen: The goal is subjective, like "cleaner code": use ak:cook.
The bug has a known root cause: use ak:fix or ak:debug.
The task is one-off with no iteration: use ak:cook.
No mechanical metric measures progress: use ak:cook --interactive.
You want an overview of goal-directed iteration options: see ak:autoresearch.

params.name: [Goal/Metric description]
params.desc: Goal or metric in words, or the full inline config block below the command.

params.name: Goal
params.desc: Required. Human-readable improvement target, e.g. 'Increase test coverage in src/utils'.

params.name: Scope
params.desc: Required. Glob of files the loop may edit, e.g. 'src/utils/**/*.ts'. Nothing outside Scope changes.

params.name: Verify
params.desc: Required. Shell command that prints exactly one number to stdout; runs every iteration, so it passes a safety screen.

params.name: Guard
params.desc: Optional, default none. Regression check command (exit 0 = pass). Files in Guard scope are read-only.

params.name: Iterations
params.desc: Optional, default 10. Maximum iterations.

params.name: Noise
params.desc: Optional, default medium. Metric variance tolerance: low / medium / high.

params.name: Min-Delta
params.desc: Optional, default 0. Minimum improvement that counts as progress.

params.name: Direction
params.desc: Optional, default higher. Whether higher or lower is better.

params.name: Timeout
params.desc: Optional, default 30s. Deadline per verify run; overruns are logged as timeout and discarded safely.

ak-bootstrap.tagline: Start a new project from idea to running code: research, stack, design, plan, build.
ak-bootstrap.summary: ak:bootstrap takes a new-project request through brainstorm → git init → research → tech stack → design → plan → implement → test → review → docs → onboarding → report. It writes no code itself; it delegates to ak:plan and ak:cook with flags per mode (full, auto, fast, parallel). Output: a repo with running code, stack docs, wireframes, a plan in ./plans, and a getting-started guide.
howItWorks: Opening brainstorm gate (all modes): captures outcome, constraints, non-goals, acceptance criteria; reuses accepted briefs; asks only key decisions.
Step 0 git init: inspects the target; reuses an existing project without re-scaffolding or resetting; inits git only for new projects.
Selects the workflow by mode: --full (default), --auto, --fast, or --parallel.
Full: clarifies one question at a time → parallel researchers (≤150-line reports) → 2-3 stack options written to ./docs.
Full then offers optional design: ui-ux-designer HTML wireframes in ./docs/wireframe/, logo via ak:ai-multimodal, screenshots via ak:agent-browser.
Fast: one parallel research batch (6 researchers), ungated design, then plan --fast. Auto/Parallel have no user gates for research/stack.
Planning runs /ak:plan --hard, --auto, --fast, or --parallel; --ultra swaps in /ak:plan --ultra. Plan = plan.md (<80 lines) + phase-XX-*.md.
Implementation runs /ak:cook <plan-path>, --auto, or --parallel; --yagni passes through to plan and cook.
Shared phases: tester runs real tests, debugger fixes failures, code-reviewer reviews, docs-manager and project-manager update docs and plan.
Onboarding guides the user step by step and explains safe credential setup without pasting secrets into chat.
Ends with a report and journal (unless opted out); commits/pushes only on request.
useWhen: You are starting a brand-new project from an idea.
You need a full-stack app (e.g. SaaS with auth, e-commerce with Stripe) with a plan and design.
You want a quick prototype and accept skipping the design gate (--fast).
The project is large and you want parallel agents with file ownership (--parallel).
avoidWhen: You are adding a feature to an existing project: use ak:plan + ak:cook.
You only need a plan: use ak:plan.
You only need to clarify the idea and compare directions: use ak:brainstorm.
You only need a .NET scaffold: use dotnet-claude-kit:dotnet-init.

ak-agentize.tagline: Turn existing code or APIs into an agent-friendly CLI, MCP server, or both.
ak-agentize.summary: ak:agentize wraps an existing codebase or module as an AI-agent surface: a CLI (structured output, clear exit codes) and/or an MCP server (transport, auth, protocol chosen per real consumers). It scouts exports, schemas, side effects, and credentials, builds an Agentization Map, decides the surface, then scaffolds, wraps, hardens, and packages. Not for building MCP servers from scratch (use ak:mcp-builder).
howItWorks: Phase 0 Track: records mode, owned files, acceptance checks, deploy intent, non-goals; plans multi-module or published surfaces.
Phase 1 Scout: inspects exports, schemas, callers, tests, side effects, credentials, runtime, and package manager.
Phase 2 Analyze: builds an Agentization Map (intent, operation, I/O schema, side effects, access control, consumer check).
Phase 3 Decide: records CLI/MCP/both, consumer, local/remote, auth, publish target; resolves protocol/SDK from manifests and lockfiles.
--auto decides alone; --ask interviews the user with a challenge framework.
Phase 4 Scaffold: reuses project layout and separates business logic from adapters; adds Cloudflare Workers/Docker/PaaS config when needed.
Phase 5 Wrap: CLI gets help, deterministic output, exit codes, non-interactive runs, stateless credentials.
MCP wrapping picks the transport, keeps stdio logs off stdout, and uses OAuth for remote servers; code mode only for bulk operations.
Phase 6 Harden: verifies original behavior through each adapter (schema, success/failure, mutation boundary, redaction, auth rejection); runs test/type/lint.
Phase 7 Package: hands off artifacts, examples, consumer results, decisions, limits; publishes only on request, with a receipt.
--ultra fans Phases 2-3 to 5 read-only candidates and a verifier; Phases 4-7 run once.
--advice consults kongming after Scout/Analyze, before locking decisions, before handoff, and when stuck.
useWhen: An internal library or service should be callable by agents (Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT) over MCP.
You want a CLI with JSON output and clear exit codes for headless agent runs.
A large REST/OpenAPI API needs exposing to agents through curated workflows.
You need a remote MCP server with OAuth for many clients.
avoidWhen: You are building a new MCP server for an external service from scratch: use ak:mcp-builder.
You want to expose website features to in-browser agents: use ak:webmcp.
You are writing a skill (SKILL.md), not a CLI/MCP: use ak:skill-creator.

It reads manifests, lockfiles, imports, and scripts to route by installed package and uses version-correct types and docs. TanStack Query, Table, Virtual, and generic React patterns are out of scope.
howItWorks: Reads the package manifest, lockfile, imports, and scripts to find installed TanStack packages and versions.
Routes: routes, server functions, middleware → Start reference; form state and validation → Form reference; AI chat/streaming → AI reference.
Loads versioned examples only when needed, then adapts them to the installed version.
Never hand-edits routeTree.gen.ts; edits source routes and runs the project's generator.
Verifies types, build, and affected behavior with existing scripts; Form edits never spawn a new Start app or AI chat.
useWhen: You are creating a TanStack Start project with file-based routing and server functions.
You need a complex form with Zod/Valibot validation in TanStack Form.
You want streaming AI chat in a TanStack app.
You are comparing TanStack Start with Next.js or Remix.
avoidWhen: TanStack Query, Table, Virtual: out of scope; use ak:frontend-development.
Next.js App Router apps: use ak:web-frameworks.
Generic React patterns unrelated to TanStack: use ak:frontend-development or ak:react-best-practices.

Next.js rendering/data changes load App Router, Server Components, data fetching, and optimization references.
Workspace and build changes load Turborepo setup, pipelines, and caching references.

Applies best practices: Server Components by default, loading/error states, Image component, SEO metadata, caching strategy.
Production uses the patched stable line; avoids pinning canary.

You are setting up a Turborepo monorepo with shared apps/ and packages/.

ak-payment-integration.tagline: Integrate SePay (VietQR), Polar, and Stripe: checkout, webhooks, subscriptions, QR.
ak-payment-integration.summary: ak:payment-integration implements payments with SePay (Vietnamese banks, VND, VietQR), Polar (global SaaS, Merchant of Record, automated benefits), and Stripe (Checkout, Billing, Connect, Payment Element). It keeps the current provider and API version, loads only needed recipes, and enforces payment-state invariants. Webhook signatures are verified on the raw payload, events are idempotent, and the server owns amount, currency, and status.
howItWorks: Keeps the current provider and API version unless asked to change.
For new setups: SePay for Vietnam/VietQR, Polar for SaaS/subscriptions, Stripe for enterprise/Connect.
Loads only the needed recipes from references/sepay/*, references/polar/*, or references/stripe/*.
Multi-provider orders use the unified order and currency-conversion patterns.
Implements the flow: auth → products → checkout → webhooks → events.
Verifies webhook signatures on the raw payload (sepay-webhook-verify.js, polar-webhook-verify.js) and dedupes with idempotency keys.
A client-side redirect never proves payment.
Handles duplicate, badly signed, and out-of-order events without wrong fulfillment; tests in sandbox and reports verified state transitions.
useWhen: You want VietQR bank-transfer payments via SePay for Vietnamese customers.
You sell global SaaS subscriptions via Polar with automatic GitHub/Discord benefits.
You integrate Stripe Checkout/Payment Element, Billing, or Connect.
You need safe, idempotent payment webhook handling.
Your order system supports multiple providers and currencies.
avoidWhen: Billing inside a Shopify app: use ak:shopify.
General backend APIs unrelated to payments: use ak:backend-development.

ak-shopify.tagline: Build Shopify apps, extensions, and themes with Shopify CLI, GraphQL, Polaris, Liquid.
ak-shopify.summary: ak:shopify determines whether the work is an app, extension, or theme from the request and project config, and reads the configured CLI and API versions before running commands. Apps use OAuth, webhook, and billing references; extensions use targets and extension APIs (Checkout, Admin, POS, Functions); themes use Liquid, sections, and preview. It keeps OAuth scopes minimal, verifies webhook signatures, keeps billing state server-side, and verifies on a development store or preview theme.

Reads the configured Shopify CLI and API versions before running commands.
Loads references: app development (OAuth, API, webhooks, billing), extensions (Checkout, Admin, POS, Functions), themes (Liquid, sections, deploy).
New setups use the setup and workflow recipes; scripts/shopify_init.py initializes projects when needed.
Pulls sample patterns: paginated GraphQL product queries, React checkout UI extensions, Liquid loops.
Keeps OAuth scopes minimal, verifies webhook signatures, holds billing state server-side, and uses idempotency.
Verifies on a development store or preview theme; going live needs the chosen store/theme and authorization.
Tracks and cleans up dev servers and tunnels it started.

ak-mcp-builder.tagline: Build MCP servers (FastMCP Python or Node/TypeScript SDK), starting from one complete tool.
ak-mcp-builder.summary: ak:mcp-builder builds MCP servers that connect LLMs to external services. It first defines the user task and the first tool contract, then implements one complete tool: validated input, authorized API behavior, bounded useful output. It then compiles, runs against a real client, and writes task-based evaluations. More tools are added only when the workflow needs them.
howItWorks: Defines the user task and first tool contract; checks the project's SDK, version, and transport.
Reads only the protocol/API parts that tool needs (auth, schema, pagination, errors/retry, transport), not the whole spec.
Picks the Python or Node server reference plus MCP best practices.
Implements one complete tool with accurate readOnly/destructive/idempotent/openWorld annotations, input constraints, actionable errors, cancellation/timeout.
Matches auth and scopes to the operation; annotations are hints, not enforcement.
Tests invalid, auth, pagination, and retry paths where relevant; extracts helpers only for real repetition.
Compiles or import-checks the server, runs it with a real client or harness, and confirms correct output and effects.
Writes 10 independent, read-only, realistic, verifiable, stable evaluation questions in XML; runs them with scripts/evaluation.py.
Bounds and cleans up server processes; reports the working contract, observed client results, and missing capabilities.
useWhen: You need an MCP server for an external API (GitHub, Notion, internal CRM) for agents to use.
You are writing an MCP server with FastMCP Python or the MCP TypeScript SDK.
You are designing MCP tool schemas, annotations, pagination, and error handling.
You want an evaluation suite testing how well an LLM uses your MCP server.
avoidWhen: Wrapping existing repo code or APIs as CLI/MCP: use ak:agentize.
Exposing website features to in-browser agents: use ak:webmcp.
Just calling existing MCP tools: use the runtime's native MCP tools.
Building a Google ADK agent that uses MCP tools: use ak:google-adk-python.

ak-webmcp.tagline: Expose website features as WebMCP tools for in-browser agents via document.modelContext.
ak-webmcp.summary: ak:webmcp turns website features into WebMCP tools: named JavaScript functions with descriptions and JSON Schema that in-browser agents call via document.modelContext instead of scraping the DOM. WebMCP is a W3C Web Machine Learning CG draft browser API, NOT an Anthropic MCP server. The skill covers the imperative (registerTool) and declarative (form attributes) APIs, schemas, safety annotations, cross-origin exposure, framework integration, validation, and evals.
howItWorks: Verifies the browser and API: records browser version, HTTPS/origin-isolation status, and available members.
Feature-detects the entrypoint and each member; without support, keeps the normal UI.
Plans tools: one tool per function, no overlap, a small set; prefers static registration.
Simple HTML forms that need no result read → declarative API; everything else (state, navigation, custom widgets, annotations) → imperative. Mixing is allowed.
Names tools by exact effect with positive descriptions and specific schemas.
Respects budgets: name ≤30, description ≤500, parameter description ≤150, output ≤1.5K.
Scaffolds with scripts/scaffold_tool.py and wires execute to existing app logic; validates strictly and returns short strings and clear errors.
Adds safety annotations: readOnlyHint, consequentialHint (irreversible actions), untrustedContentHint (UGC/external content).
Gates cross-origin use with exposedTo + Permissions-Policy tools, exposing only to trusted origins.
Validates with scripts/validate_webmcp.mjs (--strict turns warnings into errors), then tests with Model Context Tool Inspector and evals.
useWhen: You want AI agent tools on an existing website.
You want forms (booking, search, contact) to be agent-callable.
You want page actions (add to cart, filter products) exposed to in-browser agents with safety annotations.
You are integrating WebMCP into React/Angular and writing tool evals.
avoidWhen: Building stdio/HTTP MCP servers for an API: use ak:mcp-builder.
Running existing MCP tools: use the runtime's native MCP tools.
Browser automation or page testing with an agent: use ak:agent-browser.
Wrapping backend code as CLI/MCP: use ak:agentize.

Tool output, form values, and page text are untrusted data (indirect prompt injection risk), not instructions.
